claims.text: Cold spray can deposit AlCrFeNiSi powder without full melting.
Using cold spray instead of fusion-based additive manufacturing will mitigate residual thermal stresses in AlCrFeNiSi miniature components.
Cold spray will preserve the microstructural integrity of deposited AlCrFeNiSi.
Cold-sprayed AlCrFeNiSi components will have better mechanical properties than components made by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing.
Sub-melting AlCrFeNiSi deposition can be performed using powder-particle velocities of approximately 300–600 m/s.
AlCrFeNiSi powder below 50 µm is compatible with the proposed cold spray process.
The proposed process is applicable at near-ambient substrate temperatures.
Cold spraying will minimize remelting-induced grain coarsening.
Cold spraying will produce a reduced dislocation density in the deposited material.
Cold spraying will produce fewer porous regions while retaining a homogeneous phase distribution.
High-velocity particle impact supplies sufficient kinetic energy to create solid-state particle bonding.
Avoiding melting minimizes thermal gradients and prevents the high residual stresses associated with high-thermal-load processing.
A refined microstructure and lower defect density will yield improved mechanical performance.
Cold-sprayed miniature components will show significantly lower XRD-measured residual thermal stress than fusion-built controls.
Cold-sprayed miniature components will exhibit increased yield strength relative to fusion-built controls.
Cold-sprayed miniature components will exhibit increased ductility relative to fusion-built controls.
The intervention may be limited for intricate geometries or when particle deformation is insufficient to achieve bonding.
